title: Node drain horizon with reserved throughput lanes for maintenance windows
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: Scheduled maintenance (kernel/driver upgrades, host reboot, OS patches) causes uneven tail latency and temporary throughput degradation for Dedicated customers. Existing drain is 'all-or-none' which can spike token latency and fail SLOs during overlapping waves.

Goal: Implement a deterministic node lifecycle choreography that introduces a configurable 'drain horizon' and a concept of 'reserved throughput lanes' so that maintenance waves can proceed without violating per-customer latency SLO budgets or throughput guarantees.

What we will deliver:
- Drain horizon: a time-window (e.g., 15–180 minutes) before acceptance of new requests where nodes begin controlled soft-eviction from new sessions but continue serving in-flight KV-cached continuations.
- Reserved throughput lanes: fractional capacity reservations (tokenized slots) for high-SLO customers and internal warmup lanes to preserve tail latency during drains.
- KV cache warming choreography: background warming tasks that pre-populate KV caches on target replacement hosts during the drain horizon to avoid cold starts when requests migrate.
- Autoscaler integration: hooks to pause scaling decisions for an affected cell and apply a temporary throughput multiplier to avoid autoscaler-driven oscillation during maintenance.
- Observability + rollback: maintenance wave dashboard, SLO burn-rate alerts, and automated rollback triggers if p95/p99 or queue depth exceeds thresholds.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Reservation granularity: lanes are per-dedicated-fleet and quota-based. We prefer soft reservations (best-effort reclaimable) to hard capacity reservations to limit fragmentation.
- Warmup vs latency: aggressive warmup increases network/IO overhead; we will limit warmup concurrency per host and measure cost impact.
- Complexity: introduces new control-plane state (drain horizon windows, reservation tokens). Aim to keep the state machine small and idempotent.

Acceptance criteria:
1) Launch a staged maintenance wave in canary fleet with reserve_lanes=0.15 and drain_horizon=30m without p99 increase > 10% vs baseline.
2) KV warmup should reduce cold-start p99 by >30% for migrated sessions.
3) Autoscaler pause/unpause hooks prevent >25% oscillation in instance count during waves.
4) Dashboard surfaces maintenance wave, per-lane usage, and automated rollback link.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1 (canary): implement control-plane APIs and single-fleet test harness; run synthetic load and measure metrics.
- Week 2 (small fleets): enable reserved lanes for a subset of low-risk fleets and test KV warmup concurrency knobs.
- Week 3 (global): opt-in for high-SLA customers, run a real maintenance window (non-peak), monitor for 48h.

Links: Confluence design (iteration-1) https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/Drain+Horizon+and+Reserved+Lanes, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/1284, Dashboard proto: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/maintenance-waves/maintenance-wave-overview

Notes for reviewers:
- Pay attention to the node-state transitions and idempotency guarantees in the control-plane API.
- Security: reserved lanes are metadata-only tokens; no customer data leakage expected.

Long-term: complement with a capacity token marketplace so teams can auction unused reservation credits during off-peak windows.
